title: The electrocardiogram: waves and intervals
summary: What an ECG records, the P wave, QRS complex and T wave, and why a long PR (0.16 s normally) or QT (0.36 s normally) matters.
objectives: State what an electrocardiogram records and how its waves relate to mechanical events
Match the P wave, QRS complex and T wave to atrial and ventricular depolarization and repolarization
Give the normal PR (PQ) interval (0.16 s) and list causes of a long PR interval
Give the normal QT interval (0.36 s) and list causes of a long QT interval
takeaways: An ECG (EKG) is a record of electrical events in the myocardium; those events can be correlated with mechanical contraction and relaxation.

P wave: depolarization of atrial myocardium, signaling the onset of atrial contraction. QRS: ventricular depolarization (onset of ventricular contraction) and atrial repolarization. T wave: ventricular repolarization, preceding ventricular relaxation.

PR (PQ) interval: 0.16 s. Atria contract and begin to relax; at the end, ventricles begin to depolarize. Long PR: delayed AP conduction through damaged or dilated atria, or through the AV node and bundle (ischemia, compression or necrosis).

QT interval: 0.36 s, from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave. Ventricles complete contraction and start to relax. Long QT: abnormal APs through the ventricles from myocardial infarction or enlarged ventricles.

steps.title: What an ECG records
steps.text:
An electrocardiogram (ECG, also written EKG from the German spelling) is a record of electrical events in the myocardium. The myocardium is the cardiac-muscle layer of the heart wall. Electrodes on the skin pick up the summed action potentials of those cells as they depolarize (become positive inside) and repolarize (return negative inside).

The ECG can be correlated with mechanical events: each electrical wave is soon followed by contraction or relaxation of the chambers it belongs to. The trace does not itself measure squeeze or pressure; it measures electricity. You already know the action potentials (lesson 8) and the conduction pathway (lesson 7). This lesson is how that electricity looks on paper.

The diagram is a labelled ECG of one beat.
steps.pitfall: The ECG records electrical events, not the contraction itself. A P wave means the atria are depolarizing; atrial contraction follows that wave.

check.q: What does an ECG record, and what can those electrical events be correlated with?
check.a: Electrical events in the myocardium; they can be correlated with mechanical events (contraction and relaxation).

steps.title: The P wave
steps.text:
The first small rounded deflection of a normal beat is the P wave.

It is produced by depolarization of the atrial myocardium: the action potential spreading from the SA node across the right and left atrial walls. That electrical event signals the onset of atrial contraction (atrial systole). Systole means contraction of a chamber.

Because the atria are smaller and their walls thinner than the ventricles, the P wave is smaller than the QRS complex that follows. If there is no P wave, the atria are not depolarizing in an organized way (you will see that in atrial fibrillation in the next lesson).

check.q: What electrical event produces the P wave, and what mechanical event does it signal?
check.a: Depolarization of the atrial myocardium; it signals the onset of atrial contraction.

steps.title: The QRS complex
steps.text:
The QRS complex is the large, sharp spike in the middle of the beat. It has three named parts: a small downward Q, a tall upward R, and a downward S after the R. Not every lead shows all three, but the name QRS is used for the whole ventricular spike.

The QRS is ventricular depolarization, and it signals the onset of ventricular contraction (ventricular systole). At the same time, the atria are repolarizing. Atrial repolarization does not appear as its own wave; it is hidden inside the QRS because the much larger ventricular signal swamps it.

So one complex does two jobs on the electrical timeline: ventricles depolarize (visible) and atria repolarize (invisible here).
steps.pitfall: Atrial repolarization is not missing; it is happening during the QRS and is hidden by ventricular depolarization.

check.q: What two electrical events occur during the QRS complex?
check.a: Ventricular depolarization (the visible spike, signaling the onset of ventricular contraction) and atrial repolarization (hidden in the QRS).

steps.title: The T wave
steps.text:
The last rounded wave of the beat is the T wave. It is repolarization of the ventricles.

Repolarization means the ventricular muscle cells are restoring their negative resting membrane potential (about -90 mV in contractile cells). That electrical recovery precedes ventricular relaxation (ventricular diastole). Diastole means relaxation of a chamber.

Notice the order: electrical event first, mechanical event just after. P then atrial contraction; QRS then ventricular contraction; T then ventricular relaxation. The diagram labels each wave with the chamber and the polarity change.

check.q: What does the T wave represent, and what mechanical event does it precede?
check.a: Repolarization of the ventricles; it precedes ventricular relaxation.

steps.title: The PR (PQ) interval: 0.16 s
steps.text:
An interval is a stretch of the ECG that includes at least one wave. The PR interval (also called the PQ interval, because some traces have no distinct Q) is measured from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS.

Its normal duration in the lecture is 0.16 s. During that time the atria contract and begin to relax, and toward the end of the interval the ventricles begin to depolarize (the QRS starts). The 0.11 s AV-nodal delay you learned in lesson 7 sits inside this interval, which is why the PR is much longer than the 0.04 s SA-to-AV trip alone.

Elongation of the PR interval means the AP is taking too long to get from atria to ventricles. Causes:

1. Delay of AP conduction through the atria because of damage (for example ischemia). Ischemia is inadequate blood flow, so tissue is short of oxygen.
2. Delay of AP conduction because of a dilated atrium (a stretched, enlarged atrium: a longer path).
3. Delay of AP conduction through the AV node and bundle due to ischemia, compression or necrosis of the AV node or bundle. Necrosis is tissue death.
steps.mnemonic: PR = Pause before the Rapid ventricular spike, normally 0.16 s.

check.q: How long is a normal PR (PQ) interval, and name three causes of a long PR.
check.a: 0.16 s. Long PR: delayed AP conduction through damaged atria (ischemia); delayed conduction in a dilated atrium; delayed conduction through the AV node and bundle from ischemia, compression or necrosis.

steps.title: The QT interval: 0.36 s
steps.text:
The QT interval extends from the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave. The lecture value is about 0.36 s.

During the QT the ventricles are completing contraction and starting to relax. It therefore covers the whole electrical life of one ventricular beat: depolarization plus the plateau plus repolarization.

A long QT interval reflects abnormal action potentials through the ventricles. Two classic causes: myocardial infarction (MI), death of ventricular muscle from a blocked coronary artery (a heart attack), and enlarged ventricles, which take longer to activate and recover.

Put the two intervals side by side on the diagram: PR 0.16 s (atrial time plus the AV delay); QT 0.36 s (ventricular electrical time). Those two numbers are exam favourites.
steps.clinical: A long QT is not just a tracing curiosity: abnormal ventricular APs raise the risk of dangerous ventricular arrhythmias.

check.q: How long is a normal QT interval, and what two conditions produce a long QT?
check.a: About 0.36 s. A long QT reflects abnormal ventricular APs from myocardial infarction or enlarged ventricles.

steps.title: One beat on the ECG, start to finish
steps.text:
Read one normal cycle off the diagram in order.

P wave (atrial depolarization) → atria begin to contract. PR interval (0.16 s): atria contract and begin to relax; at the end the ventricles start to depolarize. QRS complex: ventricular depolarization (and hidden atrial repolarization) → ventricles begin to contract. QT interval (0.36 s) covers QRS through T: ventricles finish contracting and start to relax. T wave: ventricular repolarization → ventricular relaxation follows.

Next lesson applies this tracing to the abnormal rhythms in Table 20.1.

check.q: List the ECG waves in order and the electrical event each represents.
check.a: P wave: atrial depolarization. QRS complex: ventricular depolarization (atrial repolarization hidden). T wave: ventricular repolarization.

practice.q: An electrocardiogram is a record of…
choices: Heart sounds at the chest wall
practice.why: The ECG records electrical events in the myocardium; those events can be correlated with mechanical ones.

practice.q: The P wave represents…
practice.why: The P wave is atrial myocardial depolarization and signals the onset of atrial contraction.

practice.q: During the QRS complex, which is TRUE?
choices: The ventricles depolarize and the atria repolarize
practice.why: QRS is ventricular depolarization (onset of ventricular contraction) and hides atrial repolarization.

practice.q: The T wave represents…
practice.why: The T wave is ventricular repolarization and precedes ventricular relaxation.

practice.q: The lecture value for a normal PR (PQ) interval is…
practice.why: The PR (PQ) interval is 0.16 s. 0.04 s is SA-to-AV travel; 0.11 s is the AV delay; 0.36 s is the QT.

practice.q: The lecture value for a normal QT interval is…
practice.why: The QT interval is about 0.36 s, from the beginning of the QRS to the end of the T wave.

practice.q: Which is NOT a listed cause of a long PR interval?
choices: Ischemia, compression or necrosis of the AV node or bundle
Myocardial infarction producing abnormal ventricular APs
practice.why: MI (or enlarged ventricles) lengthens the QT, not the PR.

practice.q: A long QT interval reflects abnormal action potentials through the ventricles due to…
practice.why: The lecture names MI and enlarged ventricles as causes of a long QT.

practice.q: Put the ECG events of one beat in time order.
items: PR interval (atria contract and begin to relax)

practice.q: During the PR interval, what are the atria doing, and what begins at the end of the interval?
practice.a: The atria contract and begin to relax; at the end of the interval the ventricles begin to depolarize.

practice.q: From where to where is the QT interval measured, and what are the ventricles doing during it?
practice.a: From the beginning of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave; the ventricles complete contraction and start to relax.

title: Major cardiac arrhythmias (Table 20.1)
summary: Table 20.1 in full: rate problems, ectopic rhythms, blocks, and premature contractions, with every number the lecture gives.
objectives: Define tachycardia, bradycardia and the main ectopic atrial and ventricular rhythms, with the numbers in Table 20.1
Distinguish atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation on both the ECG and the pump
Compare first-, second- and third-degree AV block, including PR times and rates
Describe SA-node block, sinus arrhythmia, PACs and PVCs with their listed causes
takeaways: Tachycardia > 100 bpm; bradycardia < 60 bpm. PAT: sudden 95-150 bpm, P before every QRS, P inverted and on the T wave.
Flutter: 300 P waves/min and 125 QRS/min (2 or 3 P per QRS). AF: no P waves, normal QRS, irregular timing. VF: no QRS, no rhythmic contraction.

SA-node block: P waves stop; AV node paces; QRS and T still normal. First-degree AV block: PR > 0.2 s. Second-degree: PR 0.25-0.45 s, some P waves not followed by QRS (2:1, 3:1, 3:2). Third-degree: P dissociated from QRS; atria ~100 bpm, ventricles < 40 bpm.
PAC: occasional short intervals; P on the QRS. PVC: prolonged QRS, exaggerated voltage, inverted T; higher fibrillation risk.

steps.title: Abnormal rates: tachycardia and PAT
steps.text:
An arrhythmia is an abnormal heart rhythm. Table 20.1 groups them. Start with rate.

Tachycardia means a heart rate in excess of 100 beats per minute (bpm). Possible causes: elevated body temperature, excessive sympathetic stimulation (the fight-or-flight nerves firing too hard), and toxic conditions.

Paroxysmal atrial tachycardia (PAT) is a sudden increase in heart rate to 95-150 bpm for a few seconds or even several hours. Paroxysmal means it comes in bursts. A P wave precedes every QRS complex (so each atrial depolarization still triggers a ventricular one), but the P wave is inverted and superimposed on the T wave. Causes: excessive sympathetic stimulation, and abnormally elevated permeability of slow channels (the slow Ca2+ channels of pacemaker and plateau physiology).

The diagram puts sinus tachycardia and PAT one above the other: both are fast and regular, but in PAT the P waves are upside down and buried in the T waves.

check.q: Define tachycardia, and give the rate range and two ECG features of paroxysmal atrial tachycardia.
check.a: Tachycardia: heart rate over 100 bpm. PAT: sudden 95-150 bpm; a P wave precedes every QRS; the P wave is inverted and superimposed on the T wave.

steps.title: Ventricular tachycardia
steps.text:
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast rhythm that originates in the ventricles rather than the SA node. Table 20.1's key clinical point: it frequently causes fibrillation (the ventricles may degenerate from a fast organized rhythm into chaotic twitching).

It is often associated with damage to the AV node or ventricular muscle. Damaged muscle can become an ectopic focus: a spot that fires on its own, out of turn. On an ECG, VT is a fast run of wide, bizarre QRS complexes with no P wave in front of each one, because each beat starts in the ventricle instead of the SA node. In the diagram, compare the bottom strip (VT) with sinus tachycardia at the top, where every QRS still has its P wave.
steps.clinical: Ventricular tachycardia is an emergency precisely because it so often degenerates into ventricular fibrillation, which pumps no blood.

check.q: Why is ventricular tachycardia dangerous, and what damage is it often associated with?
check.a: It frequently causes fibrillation. It is often associated with damage to the AV node or ventricular muscle.

steps.title: Ectopic atrial rhythms: flutter and fibrillation
steps.text:
An ectopic action potential is one that starts in the wrong place (not the SA node). Ectopic APs in the atria produce two named rhythms.

Atrial flutter. Symptoms: 300 P waves/min but only 125 QRS complexes/min, so there are two or three P waves (atrial contractions) for every QRS complex (ventricular contraction). The AV node cannot pass every atrial impulse. Cause: ectopic action potentials in the atria.

Atrial fibrillation. Fibrillation means uncoordinated twitching instead of a single squeeze. Symptoms: no P waves; normal QRS complexes; irregular timing; the ventricles are constantly stimulated by the atria; reduced pumping effectiveness and reduced filling time. Cause: again, ectopic action potentials in the atria.

Flutter still has recognizable P waves (just too many). Fibrillation has no P waves at all.
steps.pitfall: Atrial flutter: 300 P/min and 125 QRS/min (2 or 3 P per QRS). Atrial fibrillation: NO P waves. Do not swap them.

check.q: Give the P-wave and QRS rates of atrial flutter, and the key ECG features of atrial fibrillation.
check.a: Flutter: 300 P waves/min and 125 QRS/min (two or three P per QRS). AF: no P waves, normal QRS complexes, irregular timing, reduced pumping and filling time.

steps.title: Ventricular fibrillation
steps.text:
Ventricular fibrillation (VF) is ectopic action potentials in the ventricles. The ECG shows no QRS complexes. Mechanically there is no rhythmic contraction of the myocardium: instead there are many patches of asynchronously contracting ventricular muscle. Asynchronous means the patches do not squeeze together, so the chamber never develops a useful pressure and no blood is pumped.

This is the rhythm that kills unless the heart is shocked back into a single electrical unit. Contrast it with atrial fibrillation, which still has QRS complexes and some (reduced) output.

check.q: What does the ECG of ventricular fibrillation lack, and what is happening in the ventricular muscle?
check.a: No QRS complexes. Many patches of ventricular muscle contract asynchronously, so there is no rhythmic contraction and no useful pumping.

steps.title: Bradycardia, sinus arrhythmia and SA-node block
steps.text:
Bradycardia: heart rate less than 60 bpm. Causes: elevated stroke volume in athletes (a large, strong heart can meet the body's needs with fewer beats), excessive vagal stimulation (the parasympathetic brake is too hard on), and carotid sinus syndrome (over-sensitive baroreceptors in the carotid sinus slowing the heart).

Sinus arrhythmia: heart rate varies 5% during the respiratory cycle and up to 30% during deep respiration. The SA node is still in charge; the rate just waxes and wanes with breathing. Cause not always known; occasionally ischemia or inflammation, or associated with cardiac failure.

SA-node block: the SA node stops driving the atria. Symptoms: cessation of the P wave; a new low heart rate because the AV node acts as pacemaker; normal QRS complex and T wave (the ventricles still activate in order from the AV node down). Causes: ischemia, tissue damage due to infarction, or unknown.

check.q: Define bradycardia. What happens to the P wave and the pacemaker in SA-node block?
check.a: Bradycardia: heart rate less than 60 bpm. SA-node block: P waves cease; the AV node becomes the pacemaker at a low rate; QRS and T remain normal.

steps.title: AV node block: first, second and third degree
steps.text:
AV node block means the impulse is delayed or stopped between atria and ventricles. There are three degrees.

First-degree. PR interval greater than 0.2 second. Every P still produces a QRS; the trip is just slow. Cause: inflammation of the AV bundle.

Second-degree. PR interval 0.25-0.45 second. Some P waves trigger QRS complexes and others do not. Ratios of 2:1, 3:1 and 3:2 P waves per QRS may occur. Cause: excessive vagal stimulation.

Third-degree (complete heart block). The P wave is dissociated from the QRS complex: atria and ventricles beat independently. Atrial rhythm approximately 100 bpm; ventricular rhythm less than 40 bpm (a slow ventricular escape pacemaker). Causes: ischemia of AV nodal fibres or compression of the AV bundle.

The block-strip diagram shows a long PR, dropped QRS complexes, and complete dissociation.
steps.mnemonic: 1st = longer PR, every P conducted. 2nd = some P waves dropped. 3rd = P and QRS ignore each other.

check.q: Give the PR (or rate) numbers that define first-, second- and third-degree AV block.
check.a: First: PR > 0.2 s. Second: PR 0.25-0.45 s, some P waves not followed by a QRS (2:1, 3:1, 3:2). Third: P dissociated from QRS; atria ~100 bpm, ventricles < 40 bpm.

steps.title: Premature contractions: PACs and PVCs
steps.text:
Premature atrial contractions (PACs). Symptoms: occasional shortened intervals between contractions; the P wave may be superimposed on the QRS complex. They frequently occur in healthy people. Causes: excessive smoking, lack of sleep, too much caffeine, alcoholism.

Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). An ectopic focus in the ventricle fires early. Symptoms: prolonged QRS complex (the impulse spreads through ordinary muscle, not the fast Purkinje network); exaggerated voltage because only one ventricle may depolarize; inverted T wave; increased probability of fibrillation. Causes: ectopic foci in the ventricles; lack of sleep; too much caffeine; irritability; occasionally coronary thrombosis (a clot in a coronary artery).

Table 20.1 is now complete: rates, ectopy, SA and AV blocks, and premature beats. Next, the mechanical cycle those electrical events drive.

check.q: Give two ECG features of a PVC, and list typical PAC causes.
check.a: PVC: prolonged QRS, exaggerated voltage (one ventricle may depolarize), inverted T, higher fibrillation risk. PAC causes: smoking, lack of sleep, too much caffeine, alcoholism.

practice.q: Tachycardia is a heart rate…
practice.why: Tachycardia is a rate over 100 bpm. Bradycardia is under 60. PAT is a sudden 95-150.

practice.q: In atrial flutter the lecture numbers are…
choices: No P waves and irregular QRS complexes
Atrial rate ~100 bpm and ventricular rate < 40 bpm
practice.why: Flutter: 300 P/min, 125 QRS/min, two or three P waves per QRS. AF has no P waves.

practice.q: Atrial fibrillation is characterized by…
choices: No P waves, normal QRS complexes and irregular timing
practice.why: AF: no P waves, normal QRS, irregular timing, reduced pumping and filling.

practice.q: Ventricular fibrillation shows…
choices: Normal QRS complexes at an irregular rate
No QRS complexes and no rhythmic myocardial contraction
A P wave before every QRS
practice.why: VF: no QRS; many patches of asynchronously contracting ventricular muscle.

practice.q: First-degree AV block is defined as a PR interval…
choices: Of 0.25-0.45 second with dropped QRS complexes
That is dissociated from the QRS
practice.why: First-degree: PR > 0.2 s (inflammation of the AV bundle). Second-degree is 0.25-0.45 s with some non-conducted P waves.

practice.q: In third-degree (complete) heart block…
choices: Every P wave is followed by a QRS
The atrial rhythm is about 100 bpm and the ventricular rhythm is less than 40 bpm
P waves cease and the AV node paces at a low rate with no QRS
The QRS is prolonged because only one ventricle depolarizes
practice.why: P is dissociated from QRS; atria ~100 bpm, ventricles < 40 bpm. SA-node block is the one where P waves cease.

practice.q: Second-degree AV block may show which P-to-QRS ratios?
practice.why: Table 20.1 lists 2:1, 3:1 and 3:2 P wave/QRS ratios for second-degree block.

practice.q: A PVC typically shows…
choices: A short PR interval and a normal QRS
A prolonged QRS, exaggerated voltage and an inverted T wave
practice.why: PVCs: prolonged QRS, exaggerated voltage (one ventricle may depolarize), inverted T, increased fibrillation risk.

practice.q: Sinus arrhythmia means heart rate varies…
choices: 5% during the respiratory cycle and up to 30% during deep respiration
practice.why: Table 20.1: 5% with the respiratory cycle, up to 30% in deep respiration.

practice.q: Order AV blocks from least to most complete interruption of conduction.
items: Second-degree (some P waves not followed by a QRS)

practice.q: What happens to the P wave in SA-node block, and what takes over as pacemaker?
practice.a: P waves cease; the AV node acts as pacemaker at a new low rate; QRS and T remain normal.

practice.q: List the Table 20.1 causes of premature atrial contractions.
practice.a: Excessive smoking, lack of sleep, too much caffeine, and alcoholism (they frequently occur in healthy people).

title: The cardiac cycle: systole, diastole and filling
summary: The heart as two pumps, systole versus diastole, passive then active ventricular filling, and end-diastolic volume of 120-130 mL.
objectives: Define the cardiac cycle, systole and diastole, and explain why blood moves from higher to lower pressure
Describe passive ventricular filling while all chambers are relaxed
Describe atrial systole as active ventricular filling, including its ECG marker and why it matters in exercise
Give the end-diastolic volume (120-130 mL) and say when it is measured
takeaways: The heart is two pumps working together: the atrium is the primer and the ventricle is the power.
Cardiac cycle: the repetitive pumping process from the onset of contraction to the beginning of the next contraction. Systole = contraction of a chamber; diastole = relaxation of a chamber.
Most filling at rest is passive: AV valves open, atrial pressure slightly greater than ventricular pressure. Atrial systole (P wave) then actively forces more blood in.

At rest atrial contraction is not necessary; in exercise the heart pumps 300-400% more blood and atrial contraction is necessary. EDV (end-diastolic volume) is 120-130 mL remaining in each ventricle at the end of filling.

steps.title: Two pumps and one cycle
steps.text:
The heart is two pumps working together. Each side has an atrium and a ventricle. The atrium is the primer: it tops up the ventricle. The ventricle is the power: it is the chamber that generates the pressure that drives blood through a whole circuit.

The cardiac cycle is the repetitive pumping process that begins with the onset of contraction and ends with the beginning of the next contraction. One cycle is one heartbeat, electrical events plus the mechanical squeeze and refill that follow.

Two words you will use constantly: systole is contraction of a chamber; diastole is relaxation of a chamber. You must say which chamber. Atrial systole and ventricular systole do not happen at the same time: the atria contract first, then the ventricles.

check.q: Define the cardiac cycle, systole and diastole. What is the atrium's role versus the ventricle's?
check.a: The cardiac cycle is the repetitive pumping process from the onset of one contraction to the beginning of the next. Systole = contraction of a chamber; diastole = relaxation. The atrium is the primer; the ventricle is the power.

steps.title: Pressure makes blood move
steps.text:
Blood moves through the circulatory system from areas of higher pressure to areas of lower pressure. There is no other driving force in this chapter. Contraction of the heart produces the pressure.

Valves exist so that when pressure reverses, blood cannot go backwards: they are one-way doors that open only when upstream pressure is higher than downstream pressure. Keep that rule in mind as filling and ejection unfold. The great veins (SVC, IVC, pulmonary veins) are the higher-pressure reservoirs that feed the relaxed atria at the start of filling.

check.q: Why does blood move through the heart and vessels, and what produces that driving force?
check.a: Blood moves from higher pressure to lower pressure. Contraction of the heart produces the pressure.

steps.title: Passive ventricular filling
steps.text:
Before a new cardiac cycle begins, all chambers are relaxed (atrial and ventricular diastole). The heart is not sucking blood in. At rest, most of the blood movement into the chambers results from greater blood pressure in the veins than in the heart chambers. That is passive filling: no cardiac muscle is contracting to pull or push it.

As blood moves into the atria, much of it flows straight on into the ventricles because two things are true:

1. The AV valves are open (the tricuspid on the right, the mitral/bicuspid on the left).
2. Atrial pressure is slightly greater than ventricular pressure.

This is passive ventricular filling. Later you will learn it accounts for most (~70%) of the ventricular volume. The cycle diagram marks this as the long filling stretch with both AV valves open.

check.q: During passive ventricular filling, what is the state of the chambers and the AV valves, and what pressure relationship lets blood in?
check.a: All chambers are relaxed; AV valves are open; atrial pressure is slightly greater than ventricular pressure, and venous pressure is greater than chamber pressure.

steps.title: Atrial systole: active ventricular filling
steps.text:
The SA node then generates an action potential that stimulates atrial contraction. On the ECG this is the P wave. Atrial contraction begins the cardiac cycle as the lecture defines it, and it actively forces more blood into the ventricles. This is active ventricular filling, also called atrial systole.

Depolarization spreads over the atria; they squeeze; that squeeze completes ventricular filling. The ventricles are still relaxed, so they accept the extra volume. The AV valves stay open; the semilunar valves stay closed.

check.q: What ECG wave marks atrial systole, and what does atrial contraction do to ventricular filling?
check.a: The P wave. Atrial contraction actively forces more blood into the ventricles and completes ventricular filling.

steps.title: When atrial contraction is and is not necessary
steps.text:
At rest, contraction of the atria is not necessary for heart function. Passive filling already puts most of the blood into the ventricles, which is why people can live with poorly contracting atria (as in atrial fibrillation) at rest, even though pumping is less efficient.

During exercise, atrial contraction is necessary. The heart pumps 300 to 400% more blood than during rest. Filling time shortens because the rate is up, so the atrial primer has to push extra volume in quickly or the power chambers start each beat under-filled.
steps.clinical: Atrial fibrillation removes the atrial primer. At rest many people cope; during exercise they lose the extra filling that atrial systole should have provided.

check.q: Is atrial contraction necessary at rest? What about during exercise, and by how much can output rise?
check.a: At rest it is not necessary. During exercise it is necessary; the heart pumps 300-400% more blood than at rest.

steps.title: End-diastolic volume: 120-130 mL
steps.text:
When ventricular filling is complete, each ventricle holds 120-130 mL of blood. That volume is the end-diastolic volume (EDV): the amount remaining in the ventricle at the end of diastole (the end of filling), just as ventricular systole is about to start.

The lecture places this number at the start of isovolumetric contraction in the next lesson: ventricular muscle has begun to contract, AV valves have just shut, and those 120-130 mL are trapped in the ventricle. Think of EDV as the full tank before ejection.

The next lesson is what happens to that volume: isovolumetric contraction, ejection, and the leftover end-systolic volume.
steps.pitfall: EDV is the volume at the END of filling (diastole), not the amount ejected. The amount ejected is stroke volume, which comes two lessons from now.

check.q: What is end-diastolic volume, and what is the lecture value?
check.a: EDV is the volume of blood in a ventricle at the end of diastole (after filling is complete); 120-130 mL.

practice.q: In the two-pump description, the atrium is the…
practice.why: The atrium is the primer and the ventricle is the power.

practice.q: Systole means…
practice.why: Systole = contraction; diastole = relaxation. Always name the chamber.

practice.q: Blood moves through the circulatory system…
choices: Only when all valves are open
practice.why: Flow is down a pressure gradient; contraction of the heart produces the pressure.

practice.q: Passive ventricular filling occurs because…
choices: The ventricles suck blood in by contracting
AV valves are open and atrial pressure is slightly greater than ventricular pressure
The atria are in systole for the whole period
practice.why: At rest most filling is passive: veins and atria are at slightly higher pressure than the relaxed ventricles, and AV valves are open.

practice.q: Atrial systole is represented on the ECG by the…
practice.why: The P wave is atrial depolarization, which stimulates atrial contraction (active filling).

practice.q: During exercise the heart pumps how much more blood than at rest?
practice.why: The lecture: 300 to 400% more blood than during rest, which is why atrial contraction becomes necessary.

practice.q: End-diastolic volume (EDV) is…
choices: 120-130 mL in the ventricle at the end of filling
practice.why: EDV is 120-130 mL at the end of diastole. 50-60 mL is ESV; 70 mL is a typical stroke volume.

practice.q: Put the filling events in order, starting with a fully relaxed heart.
items: All chambers relaxed; venous pressure fills the atria
P wave and atrial systole (active filling)
EDV of 120-130 mL in each ventricle

practice.q: Why is atrial contraction unnecessary at rest but necessary in exercise?
practice.a: At rest most ventricular filling is already passive. In exercise the heart pumps 300-400% more blood and filling time is shorter, so the atrial primer is needed.

practice.q: Define the cardiac cycle.
practice.a: The repetitive pumping process that begins with the onset of contraction and ends with the beginning of the next contraction.

Explain the dicrotic notch and why arm blood pressure reflects aortic, not ventricular, pressure
takeaways: Isovolumetric contraction: ventricles contract, AV valves shut, SL valves still closed, no volume change; EDV 120-130 mL is trapped.
Ejection: SL valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds pulmonary trunk (right) and aorta (left). Peak pressures: LV 120 mm Hg, RV 25 mm Hg. ESV leftover is 50-60 mL.
Isovolumetric relaxation: T wave, ventricles relax, SL valves close as blood starts to backflow; AV valves still closed; no filling yet.

Dicrotic notch: a slight rise in aortic pressure when the aortic SL valve closes. Arm blood pressure reflects aortic pressures, not ventricular pressures. Passive filling then accounts for most (~70%) of ventricular filling.

steps.title: Isovolumetric contraction
steps.text:
Ventricular systole starts as the AP reaches the AV node, AV bundle, bundle branches and Purkinje fibres. On the ECG this is the QRS complex. The period of isovolumetric contraction begins at completion of the QRS complex.

Ventricular muscle starts to contract and pressure inside the ventricles rises. Blood is pushed back toward the atria, which closes the AV valves. The semilunar (SL) valves were already closed from the previous diastole and stay closed. With all four valves closed, no blood flows into or out of the ventricles even though they are squeezing. Volume is constant: that interval is the period of isovolumetric contraction (iso = same, volumetric = volume). Pressure rises; volume does not.

check.q: Why is early ventricular systole called isovolumetric contraction?
check.a: The ventricles contract and pressure rises, but all valves are closed so no blood leaves or enters and ventricular volume does not change.

steps.title: The full tank is trapped: EDV
steps.text: At this moment 120-130 mL of blood remain in the ventricles from the last diastole: the end-diastolic volume (EDV). It is trapped until some valve opens. The AV valves just closed to start ventricular systole; the SL valves have not yet opened. The cycle diagram shows a flat ventricular-volume line during this short phase while the pressure curve climbs steeply.

check.q: How much blood is in each ventricle during isovolumetric contraction, and what is that volume called?
check.a: 120-130 mL, the end-diastolic volume (EDV).

steps.title: Period of ejection: 120 mm Hg left, 25 mm Hg right
steps.text:
Ventricular contraction continues until ventricular pressure overcomes the pressures in the pulmonary trunk and aorta. Then the cusps of the SL valves are pushed against the vessel walls and the valves open. Blood is ejected into the arteries.

The two ventricles do not reach the same pressure, because they pump into different circuits:

• 120 mm Hg in the left ventricle (systemic circuit, aorta)
• 25 mm Hg in the right ventricle (pulmonary circuit, pulmonary trunk)

After the first spurt, pressure starts to drop as blood leaves. The model shows the exits: aortic valve into the ascending aorta, pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
steps.pitfall: Same stroke volume from both ventricles, very different pressures. The thin right ventricle only has to beat 25 mm Hg; the thick left ventricle must beat 120 mm Hg.

check.q: What pressures open the SL valves on each side, and into which vessels does the blood go?
check.a: About 120 mm Hg in the left ventricle opens the aortic valve into the aorta; about 25 mm Hg in the right ventricle opens the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.

steps.title: End-systolic volume: 50-60 mL
steps.text:
The ventricle does not empty completely. At the end of the period of ejection, 50-60 mL remain. That leftover is the end-systolic volume (ESV): the volume in the ventricle at the end of systole.

So a typical beat starts with ~120 mL (EDV) and ends with ~50 mL (ESV). The difference will be stroke volume in the MAP lesson. For now, remember the two tank readings: full at 120-130 mL, leftover 50-60 mL.

check.q: What is end-systolic volume, and what is the lecture value?
check.a: ESV is the blood remaining in a ventricle at the end of ejection (end of systole); 50-60 mL.

steps.title: Isovolumetric relaxation
steps.text:
Ventricular diastole begins as the ventricles repolarize: the T wave of the ECG. Completion of the T wave results in ventricular relaxation. Ventricular pressure falls very rapidly, below the pressures in the pulmonary trunk and aorta.

Blood in those elastic arteries begins to flow back toward the ventricles, which closes the SL valves. That closure is the beginning of ventricular diastole. The AV valves are still closed (atrial pressure has not yet overtaken the falling ventricular pressure). With all heart valves closed, no blood flows into the relaxing ventricles. Volume is again constant: the period of isovolumetric relaxation.

check.q: What ECG wave leads to isovolumetric relaxation, and why is volume unchanged?
check.a: The T wave (ventricular repolarization). SL valves close and AV valves are still closed, so no blood enters or leaves the relaxing ventricles.

steps.title: Passive filling resumes (~70%)
steps.text:
While the ventricles were in systole, the atria were filling from the veins. Atrial pressure now rises above ventricular pressure, the AV valves open, and blood flows into the relaxed ventricles. This passive ventricular filling accounts for most of ventricular filling (70%). The remaining ~30% will come from the next atrial systole.

The cycle then repeats: P wave, active filling, QRS, isovolumetric contraction, ejection, T wave, isovolumetric relaxation, passive filling.

check.q: What fraction of ventricular filling is passive, and what opens the AV valves to start it?
check.a: About 70%. AV valves open when atrial pressure rises above ventricular pressure.

steps.title: The dicrotic notch and aortic pressure
steps.text:
Look at the aortic pressure curve on the diagrams. When the aortic SL valve closes, pressure within the aorta rises slightly. That little bump is the dicrotic notch (sometimes called the dicrotic wave). It is caused by the elastic recoil of the aorta against a now-closed valve: blood bouncing off the closed cusps briefly raises aortic pressure.

A blood pressure measurement taken in the arm is a reflection of aortic pressures, not ventricular pressures. The brachial and radial arteries are downstream of the aorta; they see the aortic pulse, including that notch, not the left ventricle's 120 mm Hg peak directly.

check.q: What is the dicrotic notch, and what does an arm blood-pressure cuff actually reflect?
check.a: A slight rise in aortic pressure when the aortic SL valve closes. Arm BP reflects aortic pressures, not ventricular pressures.

practice.q: During isovolumetric contraction which valves are closed?
practice.why: AV valves have just closed and SL valves have not yet opened, so all valves are closed and volume is constant.

practice.q: Peak pressure in the left ventricle during ejection is about…
practice.why: LV ~120 mm Hg (aorta); RV ~25 mm Hg (pulmonary trunk).

practice.q: Peak pressure in the right ventricle during ejection is about…
practice.why: The right ventricle ejects into the pulmonary trunk at about 25 mm Hg.

practice.q: End-systolic volume is…
practice.why: ESV is 50-60 mL left in the ventricle at the end of ejection. EDV is 120-130 mL.

practice.q: Isovolumetric relaxation begins when…
choices: The SL valves close at the start of ventricular diastole
practice.why: Ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure, blood starts to backflow, SL valves close; AV valves are still closed.

practice.q: Passive ventricular filling accounts for about…
practice.why: Passive filling accounts for most of ventricular filling (70%); atrial systole supplies the rest.

practice.q: The dicrotic notch is…
choices: A slight rise in aortic pressure when the aortic SL valve closes
practice.why: Elastic recoil against the closed aortic valve briefly raises aortic pressure: the dicrotic notch.

practice.q: A blood-pressure measurement in the arm reflects…
practice.why: Arm BP is a reflection of aortic pressures, not ventricular pressures.

practice.q: Put the ventricular mechanical phases in order, starting at the QRS.
Give EDV, the two ejection pressures, and ESV.
practice.a: EDV 120-130 mL; ejection LV 120 mm Hg and RV 25 mm Hg; ESV 50-60 mL.

title: Heart sounds, murmurs, stenosis and incompetent valves
summary: S1 lub, S2 dup, occasional S3, and how incompetent versus stenotic valves time their murmurs around those sounds.
objectives: Explain what produces the first and second heart sounds
Describe the occasional third heart sound
Distinguish an incompetent valve from stenosis by the timing of the murmur relative to S1 and S2
Relate each sound to the four valves on the heart model and to the auscultation diagram
takeaways: S1 (lub): AV valves and surrounding fluid vibrate as the valves close at the beginning of ventricular systole.
S2 (dup): closure of the aortic and pulmonary SL valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole.
S3 (occasional): turbulent blood flow into the ventricles, heard near the end of the first third of diastole.
Stenosis obstructs forward flow: aortic stenosis is systolic and mitral stenosis is diastolic.

steps.title: S1: the first heart sound (lub)
steps.text:
The beating heart makes sounds you can hear with a stethoscope. The first heart sound, S1, is the lub (sometimes written lubb). It is produced by the AV valves and surrounding fluid vibrating as the valves close at the beginning of ventricular systole.

That is the same moment as the start of isovolumetric contraction: ventricular pressure has risen above atrial pressure, so the tricuspid and mitral valves shut. The sound is the vibration, not a clap of leaflets in empty space. In the model, identify both AV valves: tricuspid between right atrium and right ventricle, mitral (bicuspid) between left atrium and left ventricle.

check.q: What produces S1, and when in the cycle does it occur?
check.a: Vibration of the closing AV valves and surrounding fluid at the beginning of ventricular systole (the lub).

steps.title: S2: the second heart sound (dup)
steps.text:
The second heart sound, S2, is the dup (or dupp). It is produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonary SL valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole.

That is the same moment the dicrotic notch appears on the aortic curve: ventricular pressure has fallen below arterial pressure, blood starts to backflow, and the semilunar valves shut. In the model: aortic valve at the exit of the left ventricle, pulmonary valve at the exit of the right ventricle.

Together: lub-dup is one beat. Lub (AV close, systole starts), dup (SL close, diastole starts).
steps.mnemonic: Lub = AV (low in the heart, start of systole). Dup = SL (outflow valves, start of diastole).

check.q: What produces S2, and when in the cycle does it occur?
check.a: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary SL valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole (the dup).

steps.title: S3: the occasional third sound
steps.text:
A third heart sound (S3) is only occasional. It is caused by turbulent blood flow into the ventricles and is detected near the end of the first third of diastole.

Turbulent flow is swirling, noisy flow, as opposed to smooth (laminar) flow. After the AV valves open, the rush of blood into still-relaxing ventricles can make this extra sound. It is not part of the normal lub-dup pair you are expected to hear in every adult; know that it exists, what causes it, and when in diastole it sits.

check.q: What causes S3, and when is it heard?
check.a: Turbulent blood flow into the ventricles, detected near the end of the first third of diastole.

steps.title: Incompetent valves (regurgitation)
steps.text:
A murmur is an abnormal heart sound from turbulent flow through a valve that is not working properly. One failure mode is an incompetent valve (also called valvular insufficiency): the valve does not close fully, so blood flows backwards when the valve should be closed. That backward flow is regurgitation.

The turbulence causes a gurgling or swishing sound. Timing tells you which set of valves:

• An incompetent AV valve: sound heard after the first heart sound (the valve should be shut all through ventricular systole, so the leak is a systolic murmur after S1).
• An incompetent SL valve: sound heard after the second heart sound (the valve should be shut all through ventricular diastole, so the leak is a diastolic murmur after S2).
steps.clinical: Mitral incompetence: systolic swish after S1 as blood goes back into the left atrium. Aortic incompetence: diastolic swish after S2 as blood falls back into the left ventricle.

check.q: When is the murmur of an incompetent AV valve heard, versus an incompetent SL valve?
check.a: Incompetent AV: gurgling/swishing after S1. Incompetent SL: after S2.

steps.title: Stenosis: identify the valve and the flow phase
steps.text:
Valve stenosis is an abnormally narrow opening that produces very turbulent blood flow. The lecture describes its sound as a rushing sound before the heart sounds.

Why “before”: a stenosed valve rushes while blood is being forced through it, just before the next closure sound. A narrow AV valve (mitral stenosis) rushes while the ventricles fill in diastole, before S1. A narrow semilunar valve (aortic stenosis) rushes during ejection, before S2. So aortic stenosis is a systolic murmur and mitral stenosis a diastolic one.

Compare an incompetent valve (last step): there the sound comes after the closure sound of the leaking valve.
steps.pitfall: Incompetent = leak AFTER the closure sound of that valve. Stenosis = rushing BEFORE the heart sounds. Students often reverse after versus before.

check.q: How does the lecture describe the murmur of a stenosed valve, and when do aortic and mitral stenosis murmur?
check.a: A rushing sound before the heart sounds (very turbulent flow through a narrow opening). Aortic stenosis: during ejection, before S2 (systolic). Mitral stenosis: during filling, before S1 (diastolic).

steps.title: Listening on the chest
steps.text:
Each valve is heard best at a particular spot on the chest wall, which is why heart location (lesson 1) matters for a stethoscope. The auscultation diagram marks those listening areas over the rib cage, with the sternum as the midline landmark. You are not hearing the valve at its anatomical position inside the mediastinum; you are hearing the sound where it is transmitted to the chest wall.

On the model, the four valves sit in the fibrous skeleton at the base of the heart: tricuspid, mitral, aortic, pulmonary. Match each valve to S1 (the two AV valves) or S2 (the two SL valves).

check.q: Which pair of valves closes to make S1, and which pair makes S2?
check.a: S1: the AV valves (tricuspid and mitral). S2: the SL valves (aortic and pulmonary).

practice.q: S1 (lub) is produced by…
choices: SL valves closing at the start of diastole
AV valves and surrounding fluid vibrating as the valves close at the beginning of ventricular systole
Turbulent filling near the end of the first third of diastole
practice.why: S1 is AV-valve closure (and surrounding fluid vibration) at the beginning of ventricular systole.

practice.q: S2 (dup) is produced by…
choices: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary SL valves at the beginning of ventricular diastole
practice.why: S2 is SL-valve closure at the beginning of ventricular diastole.

practice.q: S3 is…
choices: Turbulent blood flow into the ventricles near the end of the first third of diastole
practice.why: S3 is occasional and comes from turbulent flow into the ventricles late in the first third of diastole.

practice.q: An incompetent valve (valvular insufficiency) allows…
choices: Forward flow through a narrow opening
Blood to flow backwards when the valve is closed (regurgitation)
practice.why: Incompetence = leak (regurgitation) when the valve should be shut.

practice.q: The murmur of an incompetent AV valve is heard…
practice.why: The AV valve should be closed after S1, through ventricular systole, so the regurgitant swish is after S1.

practice.q: The murmur of an incompetent SL valve is heard…
choices: Before any heart sound and never after S2
practice.why: The SL valve should be closed after S2, through ventricular diastole, so the leak is heard after S2.

practice.q: Which pairing gives correct stenosis murmur timing?
practice.why: A narrowed valve produces turbulence during its forward-flow phase.

practice.q: Put the sounds of one cycle in time order, including an occasional S3.
items: S1 (AV valves close, ventricular systole begins)
S2 (SL valves close, ventricular diastole begins)
S3 (turbulent filling, end of first third of diastole)

practice.q: Why is valve identity necessary to time a stenosis murmur?
practice.a: Stenosis causes turbulence during forward flow: systolic through an aortic valve, diastolic through a mitral valve.

practice.q: The lecture describes the sound of a stenosed valve as…
choices: A rushing sound before the heart sounds
A gurgling sound after the heart sounds
A third heart sound in early diastole
practice.why: Stenosis: an abnormally narrow opening with very turbulent flow, a rushing sound before the heart sounds. Incompetent valves gurgle or swish after them.

title: MAP, cardiac output, stroke volume and cardiac reserve
summary: MAP = CO times PR; CO = SV times HR; SV = EDV minus ESV (70 = 120 minus 50); 5250 mL/min at rest; cardiac reserve.
objectives: Write MAP = CO times PR and define each term
Write CO = SV times HR and compute the resting example 5250 mL/min = 70 mL/beat times 75 beats/min
Write SV = EDV minus ESV and compute 70 mL = 120 mL minus 50 mL
Define cardiac reserve
takeaways: MAP (mean arterial pressure) is slightly less than the average BP in the aorta. MAP = CO times PR.
CO (cardiac output) is the amount of blood per minute pumped by the ventricles. CO (mL/min) = SV (mL/beat) times HR (beats/min).
SV (stroke volume) is blood pumped during each heartbeat: SV = EDV minus ESV. Lecture arithmetic: 70 mL/beat = 120 mL/beat minus 50 mL/beat. Resting CO: 5250 mL/min = 70 mL/beat times 75 beats/min.
Cardiac reserve is the difference between CO at rest and maximum CO. PR (peripheral resistance) is the total resistance against which blood must be pumped.

steps.title: Mean arterial pressure
steps.text:
Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is slightly less than the average blood pressure in the aorta. Arterial pressure rises with ejection and falls with runoff into the arterioles; MAP is the effective driving pressure for the systemic circuit, a little below a simple average of the peak and the trough because the heart spends more time in diastole than in systole.

The aorta is the vessel whose pressure MAP describes.

check.q: What is MAP relative to blood pressure in the aorta?
check.a: MAP is slightly less than the average BP in the aorta.

steps.title: MAP = CO times PR
steps.text:
The lecture equation is:

MAP = CO × PR

CO is cardiac output: the amount of blood per minute pumped by the ventricles. PR is peripheral resistance: the total resistance against which blood must be pumped. Resistance is the opposition to flow in the vessels (mainly the arterioles of the systemic circuit).

Read it as: the pressure in the arteries is what you get when a given flow (CO) is pushed against a given resistance (PR). Raise either CO or PR and MAP rises; lower either and MAP falls. The equation diagram shows this product as the top line.

check.q: Write the MAP equation and define CO and PR.
check.a: MAP = CO times PR. CO is cardiac output (blood per minute pumped by the ventricles). PR is peripheral resistance (total resistance against which blood must be pumped).

steps.title: CO = SV times HR
steps.text:
Cardiac output itself is a product:

CO (mL/min) = SV (mL/beat) × HR (beats/min)

Stroke volume (SV) is the blood pumped during each heartbeat. Heart rate (HR) is the number of times the heart beats per minute (bpm).

You can raise output by ejecting more per beat, by beating more often, or both. The next two steps put numbers on SV and then on resting CO.

check.q: Write the cardiac-output equation and define SV and HR.
check.a: CO (mL/min) = SV (mL/beat) times HR (beats/min). SV is blood pumped during each heartbeat; HR is beats per minute.

steps.title: SV = EDV minus ESV: 70 = 120 minus 50
steps.text:
Stroke volume is the difference between the full tank and the leftover:

SV = EDV − ESV

The lecture arithmetic uses round numbers from the cycle: 70 mL/beat = 120 mL/beat − 50 mL/beat. (EDV was given as a range 120-130 mL and ESV as 50-60 mL; the equation uses 120 and 50 to make a clean 70.)

So of the 120 mL that were in the ventricle at the end of filling, 70 mL are ejected and 50 mL stay behind. Anything that raises EDV (more filling) or lowers ESV (a stronger squeeze) raises SV.

check.q: Write SV in terms of EDV and ESV, and give the lecture numbers.
check.a: SV = EDV minus ESV; 70 mL/beat = 120 mL minus 50 mL.

steps.title: Resting cardiac output: 5250 mL/min
steps.text:
Plug in a typical resting heart rate of 75 beats/min:

5250 mL/min = 70 mL/beat × 75 beats/min

That is about 5.25 litres of blood per minute leaving the left ventricle (and the same volume leaving the right). The whole blood volume of an adult is roughly that order, so the heart turns the circulation over about once a minute at rest.

Memorize the chain, because exam questions will ask you to compute any missing piece:

MAP = CO × PR
CO = SV × HR
SV = EDV − ESV
70 = 120 − 50
5250 = 70 × 75

check.q: Compute resting CO from the lecture numbers for SV and HR.
check.a: 5250 mL/min = 70 mL/beat times 75 beats/min.

steps.title: Cardiac reserve
steps.text:
Cardiac reserve is the difference between CO at rest and maximum CO. At rest you saw 5250 mL/min. In exercise, rate and stroke volume both rise (atrial filling becomes necessary, sympathetic nerves fire), so maximum CO is much higher. The unused difference is the reserve: how much extra output the heart can still call on.

A trained heart often has a larger reserve: a lower resting rate with a larger SV, and more room to climb. Disease that caps either SV or HR shrinks the reserve, which is why people with heart failure become breathless on effort.

check.q: Define cardiac reserve.
check.a: The difference between cardiac output at rest and maximum cardiac output.

practice.q: MAP equals…
practice.why: MAP = CO times PR (cardiac output times peripheral resistance).

practice.q: Cardiac output is…
choices: The amount of blood per minute pumped by the ventricles
Slightly less than average aortic BP
practice.why: CO is blood per minute pumped by the ventricles. SV is blood per beat.

practice.q: Stroke volume equals…
practice.why: SV = EDV minus ESV. Lecture numbers: 70 = 120 minus 50.

practice.q: Using the lecture numbers, SV is…
practice.why: 70 mL/beat = 120 mL minus 50 mL.

practice.q: Resting CO in the lecture example is…
practice.why: 5250 mL/min = 70 mL/beat times 75 beats/min.

practice.q: Peripheral resistance is…
choices: The total resistance against which blood must be pumped
The PR interval of the ECG
practice.why: PR here is peripheral resistance, not the ECG's PR interval.

practice.q: Cardiac reserve is…
choices: The difference between CO at rest and maximum CO
practice.why: Cardiac reserve = maximum CO minus resting CO.

practice.q: MAP is…
choices: Exactly the average of systolic and diastolic aortic pressure
Slightly less than the average BP in the aorta
Measured only in the right atrium
practice.why: The lecture: MAP is slightly less than average BP in the aorta.

practice.q: Build cardiac output from volumes and rate, in computational order.
items: Minus ESV (50 mL) gives SV (70 mL/beat)

practice.q: Write the three linked equations for MAP, CO and SV.
practice.a: MAP = CO times PR; CO = SV times HR; SV = EDV minus ESV.
