title: Intrinsic and extrinsic regulation of the heart
summary: Preload and Frank-Starling, afterload, vagal acetylcholine, sympathetic cardiac nerves, and adrenal-medulla epinephrine and norepinephrine.
objectives: Define preload and state Frank-Starling's law of the heart
Define afterload and compare the heart's sensitivity to afterload versus preload
Describe parasympathetic (vagus, ACh) and sympathetic (cardiac nerves, epinephrine and norepinephrine) control
Explain adrenal-medulla hormonal control and how it differs in timing from nerves
takeaways: Intrinsic regulation comes from normal heart function: preload (stretch; Frank-Starling: greater stretch, greater force) and afterload (pressure the ventricles must produce to open the aortic valve). The heart is less sensitive to afterload than to preload.
Parasympathetic: vagus nerve secretes acetylcholine, hyperpolarizes the heart, decreases HR.

Sympathetic: cardiac nerves to SA and AV nodes, coronary vessels, and atrial and ventricular myocardium; epinephrine and norepinephrine increase HR and force, raise CO, and lower ESV (the heart empties more). Limitation: the heart still has to have time to fill.
Hormonal: epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla in activity, excitement or stress; slower to start than nerves but persists longer.

steps.title: Intrinsic versus extrinsic
steps.text:
Regulation of the heart means changing rate and force so cardiac output matches what the body needs. There are two layers.

Intrinsic regulation results from normal heart function: properties of the muscle itself (how stretched it is, what pressure it must beat against). No nerves required.

Extrinsic regulation involves neural and hormonal control: nerves and blood-borne hormones turning the same muscle up or down. We start inside the heart, then add nerves, then hormones.

check.q: What is the difference between intrinsic and extrinsic regulation of the heart?
check.a: Intrinsic regulation results from normal heart function (preload and afterload). Extrinsic regulation is neural and hormonal control.

steps.title: Preload and Frank-Starling's law
steps.text:
Preload is the amount of stretch of the ventricular walls. Filling stretches the muscle; more venous return means more stretch.

Frank-Starling's law of the heart: greater stretch (preload) means greater force of contraction. Within a normal range, a more-filled ventricle squeezes harder and ejects more, so SV rises with EDV. That is how the two sides stay matched: if the right heart suddenly sends extra blood to the left, the left is stretched more and automatically pumps extra blood onward.

The diagram plots force (or SV) against stretch (or EDV): the rising Frank-Starling curve.
steps.mnemonic: More in, more out. Stretch the tank, and it contracts harder.

check.q: Define preload and state Frank-Starling's law of the heart.
check.a: Preload is the amount of stretch of the ventricular walls. Greater stretch means greater force of contraction.

steps.title: Afterload
steps.text:
Afterload is the pressure the contracting ventricles must produce to overcome pressure in the aorta and move blood into the aorta (on the right side, the matching pressure is in the pulmonary trunk). It is the load waiting after contraction starts: the door the ventricle must push open.

The lecture is explicit: the heart is not as sensitive to afterload as it is to changes in preload. A moderate rise in aortic pressure does not drop SV as dramatically as a drop in filling would. Chronic high afterload (for example hypertension) still makes the left ventricle work harder over years, which matters in the heart-failure lesson.
steps.pitfall: Preload = stretch from filling (before the squeeze). Afterload = the arterial pressure that must be overcome (the load after contraction starts).

check.q: Define afterload. Is the heart more sensitive to afterload or to preload?
check.a: Afterload is the pressure the contracting ventricles must produce to overcome aortic (or pulmonary-trunk) pressure and eject blood. The heart is less sensitive to afterload than to preload.

steps.title: Parasympathetic: the vagus and acetylcholine
steps.text:
Neural control is part of extrinsic regulation. Parasympathetic stimulation is supplied by the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X). It decreases heart rate.

The transmitter is acetylcholine (ACh), which is secreted and hyperpolarizes the heart. Hyperpolarize means the inside of the pacemaker cells becomes more negative, so it takes longer for the pacemaker potential to drift up to threshold. Beats are fewer per minute. Force of contraction is not the main vagal story; rate is.

Find the vagus in the atlas as it descends in the neck and thorax beside the heart, and find the medulla oblongata, where the cardioregulatory neurons that drive it live.

check.q: Which nerve supplies parasympathetic control of the heart, what does it secrete, and what happens to the membrane and to HR?
check.a: The vagus nerve secretes acetylcholine, which hyperpolarizes the heart and decreases heart rate.

steps.title: Sympathetic: cardiac nerves, epinephrine and norepinephrine
steps.text:
Sympathetic stimulation is supplied by cardiac nerves to the SA and AV nodes, coronary vessels, and atrial and ventricular myocardium. So it can change rate, conduction, blood supply to the wall, and force.

The transmitters are epinephrine and norepinephrine. They increase heart rate and force of contraction. Increased HR raises CO. Increased force lowers ESV: the heart empties to a greater extent, so SV rises as well.

There is a limitation: the heart has to have time to fill. If rate is pushed too high, diastole becomes too short, EDV falls, and the gain in HR is offset by a loss of SV.

check.q: What do sympathetic cardiac nerves release, what happens to HR, force, CO and ESV, and what is the filling limitation?
check.a: Epinephrine and norepinephrine. HR and force rise, CO rises, ESV falls (the heart empties more). Limitation: the heart still needs time to fill.

steps.title: Hormonal control: the adrenal medulla
steps.text:
The same two chemicals can arrive in the blood. Epinephrine and norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla are released in response to increased physical activity, emotional excitement, or stress.

The adrenal medulla is the core of the suprarenal (adrenal) gland that sits on the kidney. On the kidney model, find the adrenal gland capping the kidney and the medulla at its core. This is hormonal extrinsic control: it takes longer than sympathetic nerve stimulation but persists longer. Nerves are fast on/fast off; adrenal catecholamines hang around in the plasma and keep HR and SV up after the nerves have quietened.

check.q: Where do hormonal epinephrine and norepinephrine come from, what triggers them, and how does their time course compare with sympathetic nerves?
check.a: From the adrenal medulla, in response to increased activity, emotional excitement or stress. They take longer to act than sympathetic nerves but persist longer.

steps.title: Putting the controls together
steps.text:
A working summary:

Intrinsic: more fill → more stretch (preload) → more force (Frank-Starling). Afterload is the aortic door; the heart cares less about it than about preload.

Neural: vagus/ACh slows (hyperpolarization). Cardiac nerves / epinephrine and norepinephrine speed and strengthen, empty the ventricle more (lower ESV), raise CO, but cannot skip filling time.

Hormonal: adrenal medulla, same catecholamines, slower start, longer last.

The next lesson is how the brain uses these levers when blood pressure, gases, ions and temperature change.

check.q: Name the intrinsic stretch law and the two extrinsic routes that raise HR and force.
check.a: Frank-Starling (greater preload, greater force). Extrinsic: sympathetic cardiac nerves, and epinephrine/norepinephrine from the adrenal medulla.

practice.q: Preload is…
choices: Aortic pressure the ventricle must overcome
The amount of stretch of the ventricular walls
practice.why: Preload = stretch of the ventricular walls. Afterload = pressure that must be overcome to eject.

practice.q: Frank-Starling's law of the heart states that…
choices: Greater stretch (preload) means greater force of contraction
practice.why: Greater preload (stretch) produces greater force of contraction.

practice.q: Afterload is…
choices: The stretch of the ventricular walls
The pressure the contracting ventricles must produce to overcome aortic pressure and eject
practice.why: Afterload is the arterial pressure that must be overcome to open the SL valves and move blood out.

practice.q: The heart is…
choices: More sensitive to afterload than to preload
Not as sensitive to afterload as it is to changes in preload
practice.why: The lecture: the heart is not as sensitive to afterload as to preload.

practice.q: Parasympathetic supply to the heart is the…
choices: Vagus nerve secreting acetylcholine, which hyperpolarizes the heart and decreases HR
practice.why: Vagus, ACh, hyperpolarization, decreased HR.

practice.q: Sympathetic stimulation of the heart…
choices: Increases HR and force, raises CO, and lowers ESV
practice.why: Epinephrine and norepinephrine increase HR and force, increase CO, empty the heart more (lower ESV). Limitation: time to fill.

practice.q: Hormones from the adrenal medulla…
choices: Act faster than nerves and wear off sooner
Are epinephrine and norepinephrine; they take longer than sympathetic nerves but persist longer
practice.why: Adrenal epinephrine and norepinephrine: slower onset than nerves, longer lasting. Triggered by activity, excitement, stress.

practice.q: Order these regulators from inside the heart outward.
items: Adrenal medulla hormones in the blood

practice.q: What limitation does sympathetic speeding of the heart run into?
practice.a: The heart has to have time to fill; if diastole is too short, EDV and SV fall.

title: The heart and homeostasis: baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, ions and temperature
summary: Baroreceptors in the internal carotids and aorta, chemoreceptors for pH, CO2 and O2, and how K+, Ca2+ and temperature change heart rate and force.
objectives: Locate baroreceptors and trace their reflex through the cardioregulatory center
Describe chemoreceptor control of pH, CO2 and O2
Predict the effects of high and low extracellular K+ and Ca2+ on the heart
State how body temperature changes heart rate
takeaways: Baroreceptors in the walls of the internal carotids and aorta send sensory APs (mainly in nerves IX and X) to the cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata. Cardioacceleratory neurons raise HR; cardioinhibitory neurons lower HR. The center also influences adrenal epinephrine and norepinephrine.

Central respiratory chemosensitivity involves brainstem regions, particularly the medulla; peripheral carotid and aortic bodies sense blood gases. The lecture’s hypothalamus wording should not be used as the general location rule.
High K+: HR and SV fall; ectopic APs can cause fibrillation; heart block can occur. Low K+: cardiac muscle hyperpolarizes and HR falls. High Ca2+: greater force and lower HR. Low Ca2+: higher HR.
HR rises when body temperature rises and falls when body temperature falls.

steps.title: Baroreceptors watch blood pressure
steps.text:
A baroreceptor is a stretch receptor that monitors blood pressure in the vessel wall. The lecture places them in the walls of the internal carotid arteries and the aorta.

When BP rises, the wall stretches and the baroreceptors fire more. When BP falls, they fire less. That sensory information is sent to the cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata, which can then increase or decrease HR to bring pressure back. Follow the arterial sensors and medullary control center in the diagram.

check.q: Where are the baroreceptors that monitor blood pressure, and where do they send that information?
check.a: In the walls of the internal carotids and the aorta; sensory information goes to the cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata.

steps.title: The baroreceptor reflex wiring
steps.text:
Changes in BP stimulate the baroreceptors. Sensory neurons carrying those action potentials are found primarily in the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves (IX is named in the lecture; it is not a 3D target here). They end in the cardioregulatory center of the medulla oblongata.

That center has two halves: a cardioacceleratory center that increases HR and a cardioinhibitory center that decreases HR. Action potentials then travel from the center to the heart through the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the ANS (the cardiac nerves and the vagus you just studied). The cardioregulatory center also influences secretion of epinephrine and norepinephrine to raise HR and SV.

So a fall in BP: fewer baroreceptor APs → less inhibition of the acceleratory side → sympathetic (and adrenal) output up, vagal output down → HR and SV up → MAP up.

check.q: Name the two medullary centers that change HR, and name the two cranial nerves that carry most baroreceptor APs.
check.a: Cardioacceleratory center increases HR; cardioinhibitory center decreases HR. Sensory APs travel mainly in glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X).

steps.title: Chemoreceptors: pH and CO2
steps.text:
Chemoreceptor reflexes regulate heart activity to keep pH and blood gases in their normal ranges.

The lecture puts the chemoreceptors that measure pH and CO2 in the hypothalamus; that is the answer the exam expects. (Most physiology texts place these central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata, beside the cardioregulatory and respiratory centers. Both are shown here: the hypothalamus above, the medulla below it in the brainstem.)

Rising CO2 or falling pH signals that the tissues are not being cleared fast enough, so the reflex speeds the heart and breathing.

check.q: According to the lecture, where are the chemoreceptors that measure pH and CO₂?
check.a: In the hypothalamus (lecture). Most physiology texts place these central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata.

steps.title: Chemoreceptors: oxygen
steps.text:
Chemoreceptors that monitor O2 levels sit in the aorta and internal carotids, the same large arteries that hold baroreceptors. They are sensing dissolved oxygen in arterial blood heading to the body and brain.

Prolonged lowered O2 levels cause increased HR, which increases blood pressure and delivers more O2 to the tissues. The heart is being used as a delivery pump: faster circulation when the arterial oxygen content is low for a long time.

check.q: Where are O2 chemoreceptors, and what does prolonged low O2 do to HR and BP?
check.a: In the aorta and internal carotids. Prolonged low O2 increases HR, which increases BP and delivers more O2 to the tissues.

steps.title: Potassium
steps.text:
The resting membrane potential of cardiac cells depends on K+ permeability, so extracellular potassium has powerful effects.

Increased K+ decreases HR. Both HR and SV decrease. Ectopic action potentials can result in fibrillation. Heart block (loss of AP conduction through the heart) can occur. Too much potassium outside makes the electrical system unreliable: slower, weaker, and prone to block or chaos.

Decreased K+ causes hyperpolarization of cardiac muscle and decreases HR. The inside becomes even more negative, so pacemaker cells take longer to reach threshold.

Notice both high and low K+ slow the rate, but high K+ is the dangerous one for block and fibrillation.

Course simplification: these rate arrows summarize the supplied lecture. Both high and low potassium can cause dangerous rhythm disturbances; effects vary with concentration and context.
steps.pitfall: Both high and low potassium can disturb rhythm. The lecture’s rate arrows are simplified and do not define every clinical response.

check.q: What does high extracellular K+ do to HR, SV and rhythm? What does low K+ do?
check.a: High K+: HR and SV decrease; ectopic APs can cause fibrillation; heart block can occur. Low K+: cardiac muscle hyperpolarizes and HR decreases.

steps.title: Calcium and temperature
steps.text:
Increased Ca2+ produces a greater force of contraction and a decreased HR. Extra calcium is extra trigger for the myofilaments (remember CICR from lesson 8), so the squeeze is stronger, but rate falls.

Decreased Ca2+ increases HR.

Temperature: HR increases when body temperature increases, and HR decreases when body temperature decreases. That matches tachycardia from elevated body temperature in Table 20.1. Fever speeds the pacemaker; hypothermia slows it.

The hypothalamus (shown) is the body’s thermostat.

check.q: How do high Ca2+, low Ca2+, high temperature and low temperature each change the heart?
check.a: High Ca2+: greater force and lower HR. Low Ca2+: higher HR. High body temperature: higher HR. Low body temperature: lower HR.

steps.title: A homeostatic map
steps.text:
Stack the sensors:

Pressure: baroreceptors in internal carotids and aorta → IX and X → medullary cardioregulatory center → sympathetic or parasympathetic out, plus adrenal catecholamines.

Gases and pH: pH/CO2 sensors (lecture: hypothalamus; most texts: medulla); aortic and carotid O2 sensors. Prolonged hypoxia raises HR and BP.

Ions and heat: K+ and Ca2+ change excitability and force; temperature changes rate in the same direction as the temperature change.

Last lesson of the chapter: what aging and disease do when these systems cannot keep up.

check.q: Where does the lecture place the baroreceptors, the O₂ chemoreceptors and the pH/CO₂ chemoreceptors?
check.a: Baroreceptors: walls of the internal carotids and aorta. O₂ chemoreceptors: aorta and internal carotids. pH/CO₂ chemoreceptors: hypothalamus (most texts say the medulla).

practice.q: Baroreceptors that monitor BP are in the walls of the…
practice.why: Baroreceptors are in the walls of the internal carotids and the aorta.

practice.q: The cardioregulatory center is in the…
practice.why: Sensory information goes to the cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata.

practice.q: The cardioacceleratory center…
practice.why: Cardioacceleratory = increases HR; cardioinhibitory = decreases HR.

practice.q: According to the lecture, the chemoreceptors that measure pH and CO2 are in the…
practice.why: The lecture says the hypothalamus. (Most physiology texts place these central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata.)

practice.q: Prolonged lowered O2 levels…
choices: Cause increased HR, which increases BP and delivers more O2 to tissues
Have no effect on the heart
practice.why: Prolonged hypoxia raises HR, which raises BP and O2 delivery.

practice.q: Increased extracellular K+…
choices: Decreases HR and SV and can cause ectopic APs, fibrillation and heart block
Increases force with no rate change
practice.why: High K+: HR and SV down; ectopic APs can fibrillate; heart block can occur.

practice.q: Decreased extracellular K+…
choices: Depolarizes cardiac muscle and raises HR
Hyperpolarizes cardiac muscle and decreases HR
practice.why: Low K+ hyperpolarizes cardiac muscle and decreases HR.

practice.q: Increased extracellular Ca2+ produces…
choices: Greater force of contraction and decreased HR
practice.why: High Ca2+: greater force, lower HR. Low Ca2+: higher HR.

practice.q: Heart rate when body temperature falls…
practice.why: HR increases when body temperature increases and decreases when body temperature decreases.

practice.q: Order the baroreceptor reflex from sensor to heart.
items: Baroreceptors in internal carotids and aorta
Sensory APs in nerves IX and X
Cardioregulatory center in the medulla oblongata
Sympathetic or parasympathetic outflow to the heart

practice.q: Where are O2 chemoreceptors, and what does prolonged low O2 do?
practice.a: Aorta and internal carotids. Prolonged low O2 increases HR, which increases BP and delivers more O2 to the tissues.

title: Aging, Table 20.2 diseases, and congestive heart failure
summary: Age-related changes in the heart, every condition in Table 20.2, and left-sided versus right-sided congestive heart failure.
objectives: List the age-related changes in the heart
Describe each Table 20.2 inflammatory, ischemic and congenital condition
Contrast left-sided and right-sided congestive heart failure
State how failure of one side affects the other and name the treatments given
takeaways: Aging (more obvious with exercise or other disease): LV hypertrophy, increased aortic pressure, lipid in myocardial cells, lower maximum HR, weaker hormone effects, less flexible valves, more arrhythmias, congestive heart disease, coronary artery disease.

Table 20.2 inflammation: endocarditis (valves), pericarditis, cardiomyopathy (all chambers enlarge, may lead to CHF), rheumatic heart disease after streptococcal infection. Ischemia: coronary heart disease, coronary thrombosis, myocardial infarction (heart attack).

Congenital: septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus (aorta to pulmonary trunk, lung damage, LV works harder), valve stenosis or incompetence, cyanosis (blue skin from low peripheral O2). Heart failure in the table: progressive weakening; hypertension raises afterload.

Left-sided CHF: pulmonary congestion (blood backs up in the lungs). Right-sided: peripheral congestion (blood pools in organs, edema). Either side eventually weakens the other (decompensated heart). Treat by removing fluid and with drugs that reduce afterload and increase contractility.

steps.title: Effects of aging on the heart
steps.text:
Age-related changes are more significant with exercise or other age-related diseases. The lecture list:

1. Hypertrophy of the left ventricle (the wall thickens, usually because it has been pumping against a stiffer, higher-pressure aorta).
2. Increased pressure in the aorta.
3. Lipid collection in myocardial cells (fat building up inside the muscle cells).
4. Maximum HR decreases.
5. Hormone effects decrease (the same adrenal catecholamines do less).
6. Valves become less flexible.
7. Increased arrhythmias.
8. Congestive heart disease.
9. Coronary artery disease.

Several of these feed each other: a less flexible aorta raises afterload, the left ventricle hypertrophies, maximum rate and hormone response fall, and reserve shrinks.

check.q: List at least six age-related changes in the heart.
check.a: LV hypertrophy; increased aortic pressure; lipid in myocardial cells; lower maximum HR; decreased hormone effects; less flexible valves; more arrhythmias; congestive heart disease; coronary artery disease.

steps.title: Table 20.2: inflammation of heart tissue
steps.text:
Table 20.2 groups representative diseases. First, inflammation of heart tissue.

Endocarditis: inflammation of the endocardium. It affects the valves more severely than other areas of the endocardium and may lead to scarring, causing stenosed or incompetent valves.

Pericarditis: inflammation of the pericardium (the sac from lesson 2).

Cardiomyopathy: disease of the myocardium of unknown cause, or occurring secondarily to other disease. It results in weakened cardiac muscle, causing all chambers of the heart to enlarge, and may eventually lead to congestive heart failure.

Rheumatic heart disease: results from a streptococcal infection in young people. A toxin produced by the bacteria can cause rheumatic fever several weeks after the infection that can result in rheumatic endocarditis.
steps.clinical: A strep throat in a child is not a heart disease, but the delayed toxin-triggered rheumatic fever can scar valves for life.

check.q: Which layer does endocarditis attack most severely, and what is cardiomyopathy's effect on the chambers?
check.a: Endocarditis hits the valves hardest (scarring can stenose or make them incompetent). Cardiomyopathy weakens muscle so all chambers enlarge and may lead to CHF.

steps.title: Table 20.2: reduced blood flow to cardiac muscle
steps.text:
Three named conditions starve the myocardium.

Coronary heart disease: reduces the amount of blood the coronary arteries can deliver to the myocardium.

Coronary thrombosis: formation of a blood clot in a coronary artery. A thrombus is a clot formed in place.

Myocardial infarction: damaged cardiac muscle tissue resulting from lack of blood flow to the myocardium; often referred to as a heart attack. Infarction means tissue death from lost blood supply. The anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex arteries on the model are the left-sided vessels whose blockage classically infarcts the left ventricle.

check.q: Distinguish coronary heart disease, coronary thrombosis and myocardial infarction.
check.a: Coronary heart disease: reduced delivery of blood through the coronary arteries. Thrombosis: a clot forming in a coronary artery. MI: damaged (dead) myocardium from lack of blood flow; a heart attack.

steps.title: Congenital: septal defect and patent ductus arteriosus
steps.text:
Congenital heart diseases occur at birth.

Septal defect: a hole in the septum between the left and right sides of the heart, allowing blood to flow from one side to the other and greatly reducing the heart's pumping effectiveness. The model shows the interventricular and interatrial septa, The fossa ovalis, the sealed fetal foramen ovale, is a dip in the interatrial septum rather than a separate part.

Patent ductus arteriosus: the ductus arteriosus fails to close after birth, allowing blood to flow from the aorta to the pulmonary trunk under a higher pressure, which damages the lungs. Also, the left ventricle must work harder to maintain adequate systemic pressure. Patent means still open.

check.q: What is a septal defect? In patent ductus arteriosus, which way does blood flow and who is harmed?
check.a: A hole in the septum between left and right sides, so blood crosses and pumping effectiveness falls. PDA: aorta to pulmonary trunk at high pressure, damaging the lungs; the left ventricle works harder.

steps.title: Congenital valves, cyanosis, and heart failure in the table
steps.text:
Stenosis of the heart valve: a narrowed opening through one or more of the heart valves. Aortic or pulmonary semilunar stenosis increases the heart's workload. Bicuspid (mitral) valve stenosis causes blood to back up in the left atrium and lungs, resulting in edema of the lungs. Tricuspid valve stenosis causes similar backup and edema in the peripheral tissues.

Incompetent heart valve: valves do not close correctly, and blood flows through in the reverse direction (the regurgitation you timed to S1/S2).

Cyanosis (sigh-ah-NOH-sis; cyan = blue + osis = condition of): a symptom of inadequate heart function in babies with congenital heart disease; the infant's skin appears blue because of low oxygen levels in the blood in peripheral blood vessels.

Heart failure in Table 20.2: progressive weakening of the heart muscle, reducing the heart's pumping action. Hypertension leading to heart failure is due to increased afterload. Other listed contributors: advanced age, malnutrition, chronic infections, toxins, severe anemias, hyperthyroidism, and hereditary factors.

check.q: Where does blood back up in mitral stenosis versus tricuspid stenosis? What is cyanosis?
check.a: Mitral stenosis: left atrium and lungs (pulmonary edema). Tricuspid stenosis: peripheral tissues (edema). Cyanosis: blue skin in babies with congenital heart disease from low oxygen in peripheral blood.

steps.title: Congestive heart failure: left versus right
steps.text:
Congestive heart failure (CHF) means the pump is failing and blood is backing up behind it. Either side of the heart can be affected.

Left-sided failure results in pulmonary congestion: blood backs up in the lungs. The left heart cannot accept pulmonary venous return, so the lung vessels overfill. The patient is short of breath; fluid sits in the alveoli.

Right-sided failure results in peripheral congestion: blood pools in body organs, causing edema (swelling from fluid in the tissues). The right heart cannot accept systemic venous return, so the liver, spleen, kidneys and dependent skin congest.

The diagram splits those two backup circuits: the left side backs up into the lungs; the right side backs up into the liver, spleen, kidneys and legs.
steps.pitfall: Left-sided failure congests the LUNGS. Right-sided failure congests the BODY. Students swap these constantly.

check.q: Where does blood back up in left-sided versus right-sided CHF?
check.a: Left-sided: pulmonary congestion (blood backs up in the lungs). Right-sided: peripheral congestion (blood pools in body organs, causing edema).

steps.title: Decompensation and treatment
steps.text:
Failure of either side ultimately weakens the other side. Left failure floods the lungs, raises pulmonary pressure, and overloads the right ventricle. Right failure starves the left of output and raises systemic venous pressure. The result is a decompensated, seriously weakened heart: compensation (Frank-Starling, hypertrophy, extra sympathetic drive) has run out.

Treatment: removal of fluid, and drugs to reduce afterload and increase contractility. Lowering afterload makes it easier for a weak ventricle to eject; increasing contractility raises SV and lowers ESV; taking fluid off reduces the congested backup.

That is the end of Chapter 20: from where the heart sits, through its wall, valves, electricity, ECG, cycle, sounds, equations and controls, to aging and failure.

check.q: What happens if only one side fails for long enough, and what three treatments does the lecture name?
check.a: Failure of either side ultimately weakens the other, producing a decompensated, seriously weakened heart. Treatment: remove fluid; drugs that reduce afterload; drugs that increase contractility.

practice.q: Which is NOT a listed age-related change of the heart?
practice.why: Maximum HR decreases with age, it does not increase.

practice.q: Endocarditis affects which structures most severely?
practice.why: Endocarditis affects the valves more severely than other endocardium and may scar them stenosed or incompetent.

practice.q: Cardiomyopathy results in…
choices: Weakened cardiac muscle with all chambers enlarging, and may lead to CHF
A clot in a coronary artery
Blue skin in an infant only
practice.why: Cardiomyopathy weakens myocardium, all chambers enlarge, may lead to congestive heart failure.

practice.q: Myocardial infarction is…
choices: Damaged cardiac muscle from lack of blood flow to the myocardium; a heart attack
practice.why: MI = damaged myocardium from lost blood flow; often called a heart attack.

practice.q: In patent ductus arteriosus, blood flows from…
choices: Aorta to pulmonary trunk under higher pressure, damaging the lungs
Right atrium to left atrium only
The coronary sinus to the SVC
practice.why: The open ductus lets aortic blood enter the pulmonary trunk at high pressure; the lungs are damaged and the LV works harder.

practice.q: Mitral (bicuspid) stenosis backs blood up into the…
choices: Left atrium and lungs, causing pulmonary edema
practice.why: Bicuspid stenosis: backup in the left atrium and lungs, pulmonary edema. Tricuspid stenosis: peripheral edema.

practice.q: Left-sided congestive heart failure results in…
choices: Peripheral congestion and organ edema only
Pulmonary congestion (blood backs up in the lungs)
practice.why: Left-sided failure: pulmonary congestion. Right-sided: peripheral congestion.

practice.q: Right-sided congestive heart failure results in…
choices: Peripheral congestion: blood pools in body organs, causing edema
practice.why: Right-sided failure pools blood in the body organs (edema).

practice.q: Lecture treatment of a decompensated failing heart includes…
choices: Removal of fluid and drugs that reduce afterload and increase contractility
Always closing a ductus arteriosus first
practice.why: Remove fluid; drugs to reduce afterload and increase contractility.

practice.q: Cyanosis in a baby with congenital heart disease is…
choices: Blue skin from low oxygen in peripheral blood
Always caused by mitral stenosis in adults
practice.why: Cyanosis: infant skin appears blue because of low O2 in peripheral blood vessels.

practice.q: Order the backup of left-sided then right-sided failure.
items: Left ventricle fails to accept pulmonary venous return
Right ventricle is overloaded and fails

practice.q: Name the four inflammatory Table 20.2 conditions of heart tissue.
practice.a: Endocarditis, pericarditis, cardiomyopathy, and rheumatic heart disease.
